turns.text: Turn this article into a roughly 90-second podcast chat between two hosts. Use two clearly different English voices, one male and one female, friendly and curious rather than newsreader-ish. Explain what tiny urban forests are and discuss the article's main points without making up facts. No music. Please give me the finished audio, not just a script.

answer_sheet.Wording and factual scope: Wording is your call. Explain tiny urban forests and discuss the article's main points, using only facts supported by the attachment.

must_haves: The delivered file is playable audio lasting 60–120 seconds, targeting approximately 90 seconds.
Two clearly distinguishable voices, one male and one female, take multiple conversational turns.
The conversation explains tiny urban forests as dense plantings in small urban spaces and covers the attached article's main points.
Factual claims are supported by the article, with no invented statistics, studies, quotations, or named examples.
The hosts sound friendly and curious, responding to one another rather than simply splitting a straight article reading.
Speech is intelligible throughout, with no music, truncated words, or distracting joins between turns.

Why cities are planting tiny forests

Across Europe and Asia, cities are turning empty lots the size of a tennis court into dense "tiny forests". args.name: Tiny Urban Forests — Two-Host Podcast Attempt

style.prompt: No music. Create a roughly 90-second spoken-word podcast conversation in English between two distinct adult hosts. Speech only, completely unaccompanied: no instruments, no soundtrack, no beats, no melody, no singing or chanting. Natural conversational speaking with short pauses. Alternate speakers at the HOST ONE and HOST TWO markers in the supplied text, but do not say the markers aloud. Read the supplied dialogue faithfully without adding facts or extra commentary. Clear dry studio voices, conversational delivery.
style.lyrics:
[HOST ONE — spoken]
A forest the size of a tennis court? That’s the idea behind tiny urban forests. Across Europe and Asia, cities are turning empty lots into dense patches of trees.

[HOST TWO — spoken]
The method was developed by Japanese botanist Akira Miyawaki. It involves planting three to five native saplings per square metre, in enriched soil.

[HOST ONE — spoken]
Three to five in a single square metre sounds crowded. What’s the thinking?

[HOST TWO — spoken]
The trees compete for light and grow quickly. Supporters say a tiny forest can become self-sustaining in about three years.

[HOST ONE — spoken]
And advocates point to cooler streets, more insects and birds, and places where schoolchildren can learn.

[HOST TWO — spoken]
But critics say the evidence is still thin. Many projects are too young to measure, and dense planting can mean many saplings die.

[HOST ONE — spoken]
So there are promising claims, but also uncertainties about the results.

[HOST TWO — spoken]
Exactly. And urban ecologists agree on one important point: tiny forests are not a substitute for protecting existing large trees.

[HOST ONE — spoken]
Because those large trees store far more carbon.

[HOST TWO — spoken]
That’s the key distinction: planting a tiny forest does not replace protecting the big trees already there.
